title: Anti-Corruption After The Plenum

Anti-Corruption After The Plenum

Andrew Batson

Gavekal Dragonomics | 30 Oct 2026

2026 has been another extraordinarily busy year for the Communist Party’s anti-corruption investigators. The Central Commission for Discipline Inspection is still churning through tens of thousands of cases every month, including those of high-ranking current and former officials—underscoring once again that no one is safe from its reach. All this effort is aimed not only at rooting out financial impropriety but also at building a system for enforcing compliance with central directives, which top leader Xi Jinping sees as a widespread problem. He has devoted the Party’s Fifth Plenum, which concluded Thursday in Beijing, to “advancing full and rigorous Party self-governance,” meaning how the Party selects, manages and disciplines officials.The most important issue for Xi is the effective top-down transmission of orders. “Implementing the major decisions and plans of the Party Central Committee is a basic requirement of the Party’s political discipline and political rules,” Xi said in a speech to the CCDI in January, which was published in full shortly before the plenum. “We cannot merely shout slogans, still less say one thing and do another. Anyone who violates these requirements must be held accountable.” The transformation of anti-corruption into a system of political supervision, already well advanced, was confirmed by the plenum, which agreed to “integrate conduct improvement and discipline enforcement with anti-corruption measures.”
